source.title: Long Is More Important Than Difficult for Training Reasoning Models
source.authors: Si Shen; Fei Huang; Zhi-Xiao Zhao; Chang Liu; Tian Zheng; Dan-Hao Zhu

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures benchmark accuracy after training with different reasoning-data lengths, not held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or compute. It neither tests nor relies on the claim’s scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a separate relationship between reasoning-data length and benchmark accuracy. These results do not measure the loss, model/token/compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, architecture sensitivity, or downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss specified by the claim versions. Rows below record the adjacent reasoning-length result with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper fine-tunes one model, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, on 300-sample datasets whose reasoning-trace length varies from 1.5k to 12k tokens. It reports benchmark accuracy, which it calls log-linear in length and labels a 'scaling law'. It does not measure held-out loss, does not vary parameters or compute, does not fit a power law to loss, and does not relate downstream performance to model scale or pretraining loss. Kaplan et al. appear only in related work. The result is an adjacent construct (accuracy vs. fine-tuning trace length), not a test of any version. V5 (fine-tuning regimes) does not apply, because the measure is accuracy rather than loss and no power-law form is fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that reasoning length, not problem difficulty, mainly drives the performance of fine-tuned reasoning models. They report accuracy growing log-linearly (nearly linearly as length grows exponentially) with training reasoning length. They also present Long1K-32B, trained on 1k synthesized concatenated samples, as reaching 95.6% on MATH500 and 71.1% on GPQA Diamond.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies the length of reasoning data in fine-tuning and reports task accuracy; it does not reproduce the original loss-scaling methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported benchmark accuracy changes across reasoning-data lengths of 1.5k, 3k, 6k, and 12k.

fits_no_version.finding: With difficulty held constant and 300 training samples, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct fine-tuned on longer reasoning traces (1.5k to 12k tokens) gains accuracy: MATH500 rises from 87.6% to nearly 93%, GPQA Diamond from 56.9% to over 63%. The authors describe the rise as roughly linear in log length.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-task accuracy after SFT rises log-linearly with the reasoning-trace length of the fine-tuning data (one model, four length levels).

record.problems: The reasoning-length scaling result uses one model and 300 training samples per dataset. The text says results are averages of five trials, but gives no uncertainty estimates. The intermediate plotted values are not stated in text.
record.rows_left_out: Long-versus-difficult training comparisons and the Long1K-32B benchmark comparisons in Table 3 were left out because they do not measure any claim version’s loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, or downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss, no parameter, token or compute sweep.
All: no extrapolation of fitted laws to larger runs.
Power-law loss in fine-tuning. Only accuracy vs. trace length is reported, with no loss and no power-law fit.
Downstream performance vs. model scale or pretraining loss. Only fine-tuning data length varies; 7B vs 32B appears only in the length-vs-difficulty comparison, with no scale trend.
All: no exponent or fitting-choice analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R1–R8 are correctly linked to 'none'. Their values are sweep endpoints only; the intermediate points (R2, R3, R6, R7) are figure-only. The evidence is thin: one model, four length levels, no stated uncertainty despite five-trial averages, and no fitted slope reported. Total training tokens also grow with trace length, so length and data volume are confounded. The paper's 'scaling law' is a naming overlap with the claim, not a loss power law.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power-law fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the claimed loss power law holds across modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of the claimed loss exponents or compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.
